Surah Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him

It is Makkī by consensus, and it has twenty-eight verses according to the Kufan count, nine according to the Basran and Shamī counts, and thirty in all other reckonings. As for its connection (wajh al-ittisal) with what precedes it, according to what al-Jalal al-Suyuti said, and others have alluded to the same, when Allah, Glorified is He, said in Surah al-Ma'arij, ﴿Indeed, We are able﴾ ﴿to replace them with better than them﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 40, 41], He followed it with the story of the people of Noah, peace be upon him, which includes their drowning, every last one of them, such that no dweller of the earth from among them remained, and He replaced them with better than them. Thus it serves as evidence and confirmation for that claim, just as the story of the companions of the Garden in Surah al-Qalam serves as confirmation of what that surah concludes with. This is in addition to the similarity of the openings of the two surahs regarding the punishment promised to the disbelievers. The connection according to the view of the one who claims that the questioner (in al-Ma'arij) is Noah, peace be upon him, is clear. In some reports there is also what indicates that the Prophet ﷺ will recite it to the people of Noah, peace be upon him, on the Day of Resurrection.

al-Hakim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (marfu'): "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, will summon Noah and his people first among the people on the Day of Resurrection, and He will say: 'What did you answer Noah?' They will say: 'He did not call us, nor did he convey to us, nor advise us, nor command us, nor forbid us.' Then Noah, peace be upon him, will say: 'O Lord, I called them with a call that was widespread among the first and the last, nation after nation, until it reached the seal of the Prophets, Ahmad ﷺ, and he copied it, read it, believed in it and affirmed it.' Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say to the angels, peace be upon them: 'Call Ahmad and his nation.' So they will call them, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will come with his nation, their light running before them. Then Noah, peace be upon him, will say to Muhammad ﷺ and his nation: 'Do you know that I conveyed the message to my people and strove to give them sincere advice, and exerted myself to rescue them from the Fire, secretly and openly, but my call only increased them in flight?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his nation will say: '(Indeed) we bear witness to what you have recited to us, that you were in all that you said among the truthful.' Then the people of Noah, peace be upon him, will say: 'How did you and your nation come to know this, when we are the first of the nations and you are the last of the nations?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ will say: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people﴾ [Nuh: 1],' until he finishes the surah. When he finishes it, his nation will say: 'We bear witness that this is indeed the true account, and there is no god but Allah, and indeed Allah is the Mighty, the Wise.' Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say at that time: 'Separate yourselves today, O criminals.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah﴾: It is a non-Arabic name (ism a'jami). al-Jawaliqi added that it is arabized (mu'arrab), and al-Kirmani said its meaning in Syriac is "the one who rests" (al-sakin). It is declared without tanwin (ghayr munsarif) because it does not exceed three letters while its middle letter is sukun, and it is not originally Arabic at all. As for al-Hakim's statement in al-Mustadrak that he was named Noah because of his frequent wailing (nawh) and weeping over himself, and that his name was 'Abd al-Ghaffar, I do not think it is sound. Likewise what is related about the cause of his weeping, that he, peace be upon him, saw a mangy, filthy dog and spat at it, whereupon Allah made it speak, and it said: "Do you find fault with me or with my Creator?" So he regretted it and wailed for that, is also to be rejected.

It is well known that he, peace be upon him, was the son of Lamk (with a fatha on the lam and a sukun on the mim, followed by a kaf), son of Matushalakh (with a fatha on the mim, a shadda on the ta' with a damma after it, followed by a sakin waw, and a fatha on the shin, lam and the dotted kha'), son of Khanukh (with a fatha on the dotted kha', a damma on the light nun, followed by a sakin waw, then a dotted kha'; the form Akhanukh with a hamza at its beginning has also spread), who is Idris, peace be upon him, son of Yard (with a fatha on the letter ya' with two dots beneath, then a sakin unpointed ra'), son of Muhalayil, son of Qaynan, son of Anush (with the nun and the dotted shin), son of Shith, son of Adam, peace be upon him. This indicates that he, peace be upon him, came after Idris, peace be upon him.

In al-Mustadrak it is stated that most of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, held that he came before Idris. In the same work, from Ibn 'Abbas: "There were ten centuries between Adam and Noah, peace be upon them both." Also in it, traced to the Prophet: "Allah sent Noah at the age of forty, and he remained among his people for a thousand years minus fifty years, calling them. He lived after the Flood sixty years, until the people multiplied and spread."

Ibn Jarir mentioned that his birth took place one hundred and twenty-six years after the death of Adam, peace be upon him. In al-Tahdhib of al-Nawawi, may Allah have mercy on him, it is stated that he was the longest-lived of the prophets, peace be upon them. It has also been said that he was the longest-lived of all people absolutely. According to what Shaddad said, he lived nine hundred and eighty years, and no one is reported to have lived like that, meaning by consensus, lest al-Khidr be counted; but this may be answered otherwise. He is said to be the first to whom laws (shara'i') were prescribed and sunan established, and the first messenger to warn against shirk, whose nation was destroyed. The truth is that Adam, peace be upon him, was a messenger before him, sent to his wife Hawwa' and then to his sons, and in his law were those things that were abrogated by the law of Noah according to one view; according to another, there was in his law nothing but the call to faith. Noah, peace be upon him, is called the Shaykh of the Messengers and the Second Adam. He had a slender face, a long head, large eyes, thick upper arms, heavy thighs, a large navel, a long beard and stature, and a massive body.

There is disagreement about the location of his grave. It is said to be in the mosque of Kufa, it is said to be at the Red Mountain, and it is said to be at the foot of the Lebanon mountains in the city of al-Karak. As for attributing the verb to the pronoun (i.e., "We sent"), the majesty together with the emphasis of the sentence shows clearly the care given to the matter of his sending, peace be upon him. ﴿To his people﴾: It is said they were the inhabitants of the Arabian Peninsula and those near them, not the people of the entire earth, since our Prophet ﷺ is distinguished by the universality of his mission among the messengers, peace be upon them all. What was for Noah, after the story of the drowning, if we accept that his mission was universal, is an incidental matter. It is well known that he, peace and blessings be upon him, dwelt in the land of Kufa, and there he was sent. ﴿That warn your people﴾, i.e., "that warn your people."

Here "an" (أن) is explanatory (tafsiriyya), because the sending contains the meaning of saying but not its letters, so the clause has no place in terms of i'rab. Or it means "warn them," i.e., "by their warning" or "for their warning," in which case "an" is a masdariyya particle with a suppressed preposition before it, which is either the ba' or the lam; there are two well-known views about the case-position of the clause after the deletion of the genitive or accusative. Abu Hayyan explicitly permitted this possibility in his al-Bahr here, and prohibited it in another place. Ibn Hisham in al-Mughni reported the prohibition from him and said: "Abu Hayyan claimed that they (the particles) are not joined to the imperative, and that everything heard of that kind has 'an' in it as explanatory. He argued with two proofs: first, that when they are assumed as a verbal noun the meaning of the imperative is lost; second, that they do not occur as subject or object, so one cannot say 'a'jabani an qum' (it pleased me that stand up) or 'karihtu an qum' (I disliked that stand up), as can be said with the past and present tenses." The reply to the first is that the loss of the imperative meaning when assumed as a verbal noun is like the loss of the meaning of past and future in the relative clause with the present or past tense under the same assumption. Moreover, he accepts that the light (mukhaffafa) masdariyya particle carries similar implications, as in His saying, ﴿And the fifth, that the wrath of Allah be upon her﴾ [al-Nur: 9], since the supplication is only understood from the verbal noun if it is an absolute object, as in "saqyan wa ra'yan" (water and pasture). As for the second, he only prohibited what he mentioned because there is no sense in attaching liking and disliking to a performative utterance, not because of what he mentioned. Then he should not accept that "kay" is masdariyya, since it does not occur as subject or object but only in the genitive with the lam of purpose. Furthermore, what decisively refutes his view is the report of Sibawayh: "I wrote to him 'bi-an qum'" and the supposition that the ba' is extra, as some say, is a gross error, because prepositions in general only enter upon a noun or what is in the position of a noun.

Some have also answered the first objection by saying that when it is assumed, the imperative is assumed, so that it is said here, for example, ﴿Indeed We sent Noah to his people﴾ with the command to warn them. This was objected to on the ground that there is no verb whose verbal noun is the imperative, like "amrina" or "na'muru." Moreover, the meaning in such a case as "amartuhu bi-an qum" would be "I commanded him with the command to stand." Al-Zamakhshari pointed to the answer to this: when the word for command, or something with its meaning such as "rasamtu" (I drew up), has not preceded, then it is necessary to assume the verb "to say," lest the demand be nullified; so it is said here: "We sent him, saying to him, 'warn!'," i.e., "with the command to warn." But when the command has preceded, there is no need to assume it, because the resulting expressions, namely "amartuhu bi-l-qiyam" (I commanded him to stand) and "amartuhu bi-anna-hu qum" and "an qum" without the ba', are to be taken as explanatory to one thing. In al-Kashf it is said: if it were said that the assumption is "We sent him with the command to warn," without assuming a verb of saying, it would be good, because the sense of command is not the core meaning of the word but comes from the context of the particle, so it is assumed as a verbal noun in a subordinate manner. In the case of the addressed imperative, the form is sufficient for confirmation. This is like the assumption in "an la yazni" (that he not commit fornication), which is better for him, where the negation is assumed as a verbal noun in a subordinate way.

As for when the command is stated explicitly, there is no need to assume a verbal noun for the demand either. Moreover, if one assumes "amartuhu bi-l-amr bi-l-qiyam" (I commanded him with the command to stand), meaning that he should command himself with it, as an exaggeration in the demand, it is not far from the correct meaning, and since what is understood from it is what is understood from the first, and more eloquent, he used it in its usage without regard to the original. Some have also suggested that the assumption of the verb of saying here is not lest the meaning of demand be lost, but because the omitted ba' expresses accompaniment (mulabasa), and Noah's sending, peace be upon him, was not accompanied by his warning, since it came after it; rather it was accompanied by the saying of Allah, Exalted is He, to him, peace be upon him: ﴿Warn!﴾. Since this saying from Him, Exalted is He, was for seeking the warning, it was said: "The meaning is: We sent him with the command to warn." And this speaker did not mind the loss of the meaning of demand, as the words of Ibn Hisham cited just above imply.

Al-Khafaji examined what they mentioned about the loss, saying: "How can the meaning of demand be lost when it is explicitly stated in 'Warn!' and the like, and its interpretation as a verbal noun is an interpretation that does not contradict it, because it is an understood meaning taken from the sources of its usage? How then does one nullify its explicit utterance? What they mentioned has no basis, even if they agreed upon it. Understand this." End of quotation.

I say: Perhaps they meant by the loss of the meaning of demand, its loss at the mention of the verbal noun derived from the interpretation with the verb, in the sense that when it is mentioned with a verb, the meaning of demand is not realized and the two statements do not become identical; they did not mean that it is lost absolutely, for how could that be, when its realization in the explicit utterance is like a fire with knowledge? This is supported by their rejection of the invalidity of the necessary consequence pointed to in Ibn Hisham's words, that the loss of the imperative meaning when assumed as a verbal noun is like the loss of past and future meaning, etc. It is as if it were said: we do not accept that this loss is invalid; why should it not be like the loss of the meaning of past and future, and the loss of the meaning of supplication in such as "anna ghadaba" [al-Nur: 9]? They have agreed that this is not invalid, because it is a loss at the mention with the verb and is not necessary, and it is not an absolute loss, since it is evident that the explicit utterance takes charge of it. So reflect.

Ibn Mas'ud read "anzir" without "an," on the understanding of saying, i.e., "saying: warn!" ﴿Before there comes to them a painful punishment﴾: immediate, which is what befell them of the Flood, as al-Kalbi said; or deferred, which is the punishment of the Fire, as Ibn 'Abbas said. The meaning is: warn them before that, so that they have no excuse whatsoever.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verses 2–3:

﴿He said﴾ is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "What did he (peace be upon him) do after this sending?" So it was said: he said to them, ﴿O my people, indeed I am for you a clear warner﴾ — mundhir (a warner), muwaddih (making clear) the reality of the matter. The lam in (lakum) is for emphasis (lil-taqwiyah) or for causation (lil-ta'lil), meaning: for the sake of your benefit, without my asking you for a reward. And his saying, may He be exalted, ﴿that worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me﴾ is connected to nadhir (warner), with (an) being both verbal-source (masdariyyah) and explanatory (tafsiriyyah). Its parallel has passed in al-Shu'ara'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verses 2–3:

﴿He said﴾ is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "What did he (peace be upon him) do after this sending?" So it was said: he said to them, ﴿O my people, indeed I am for you a clear warner﴾ — mundhir (a warner), muwaddih (making clear) the reality of the matter. The lam in (lakum) is for emphasis (lil-taqwiyah) or for causation (lil-ta'lil), meaning: for the sake of your benefit, without my asking you for a reward. And his saying, may He be exalted, ﴿that worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me﴾ is connected to nadhir (warner), with (an) being both verbal-source (masdariyyah) and explanatory (tafsiriyyah). Its parallel has passed in al-Shu'ara'.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 4:

His saying, may He be glorified, ﴿He will forgive you some of your sins﴾ is in the jussive (majzum) as the answer (jawab) to the imperative. Scholars differ regarding "min" (from/of). It is said to be initial (ibtida'iyya, indicating a starting point), though it is not suitable here for the sense of "ila" (to), and the beginning of the action comes from Him, may He be exalted, in the sense that He, may He be glorified, begins to forgive their sins after their faith, as a benevolence and bounty from Him, mighty and majestic. It is also permitted that the beginning comes from their side, in the sense that the first thing that happens for them, because of their faith, is the forgiveness of their sins, but this is not the right view. It is also said to be explanatory (bayaniyya), and that its meaning returns to the sense of the initial; al-Radi rejected this. Before it there is an indefinite noun that is explained by what follows it, meaning: He will forgive you your actions which are the sins. It is also said to be superfluous (za'ida), according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, who permits its superfluity without restriction, and he decided this here. It is also said to be partitive (tab'idiyya), meaning: He will forgive you some of your sins, and some have preferred this view.

Scholars differ about the part that is forgiven. Some hold that it is only the rights of God, may He be exalted, that preceded faith, and others hold that it is whatever they committed before faith, without restriction. The apparent view is what has been transmitted, that faith effaces what came before it. Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam raised a difficulty about this in al-Fawa'id al-Muntashira and answered it, saying: How can this be valid according to the opinion of Sibawayh, who, unlike al-Akhfash, does not hold that it is superfluous in an affirmative statement, but says that it is for partition, while Islam effaces what came before it so that nothing of it remains? The answer is that attributing sins to them is only true in reality regarding what has occurred, for what has not occurred is not a sin for them; and attributing what has not occurred is done by way of metaphor (tajawwuz), as in ﴿And guard your oaths﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 89], where what is meant is the future oaths. Since the attribution is sometimes real and sometimes metaphorical, Sibawayh combines the real and the metaphorical in it, and this is permissible.

That is, according to its adherents among the Shafi'is, and the meaning of "some of your sins" is the part that has occurred, and it does not need the hadith of the collective (hadith al-jam') to restrict the forgiven sins to the rights of God, may He be mighty and majestic. Here there is a point of inquiry: taking it as partitive is contradicted by ﴿He will forgive you of your sins﴾ and ﴿Indeed, God forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. Al-Ba'li, in his commentary on al-Jumal, stated that this is what prompted al-Akhfash to decide that it is superfluous here, and Ibn al-Hajib took it as an argument for him. Some eminent scholars refuted this, saying that the particular affirmative proposition is a necessary consequence of the universal affirmative proposition, and there is no contradiction between the necessary consequence and that which necessitates it. The basis of this refutation is the oversight of the fact that the meaning of the partitive "min" is mere partiality (al-ba'diyya al-mujarrada) free from totality, which is incompatible with it, and not the partiality that includes what is within the whole and combined with it. Otherwise the difference between it and explanatory "min" would not be realized in terms of the ruling, and the disagreement between Imam Abu Hanifa and his two companions would not be easily applied in the case where he says: "Divorce yourself by three, as much as you wish," on the basis that "min" is partitive according to him and explanatory according to them. In al-Hidaya he said: If he says to her, "Divorce yourself by three, as much as you wish," she may divorce herself once and twice, but not three times according to Abu Hanifa. His two companions said she may divorce herself three times if she wishes, because the word "ma" is definitive in generality, and the word "min" is used for specification, so it is understood as specification of kind. Abu Hanifa's argument is that the word "min" is real for partiality, and "ma" is for generality, so both are acted upon. End of quotation.

There is no doubt that building the aforementioned answer on "min" being partitive is valid only if its meaning then is mere partiality, which excludes totality. Hence you will be surprised at the author of al-Tawdih in his presentation of this disagreement, since he argued for the preference of partition by its certainty, and did not realize that the part intended with certainty under the explanatory reading is the general part, which includes what is within the whole, not the mere part that is intended here.

By the rationale in the stated manner, the approximation is not complete; indeed there is no fit between the reason and what is reasoned, as has been said. Al-Allama al-Taftazani approved and said, having annotated it on al-Talwih, arguing that the partiality indicated by partitive "min" is the mere partiality that is incompatible with totality, not the partiality that is more general, whether it is within the whole or without it, because the grammarians agree on this, since they needed to reconcile the saying of God, may He be exalted, ﴿He will forgive you of your sins﴾ and His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, God forgives all sins﴾. They said: It is not far-fetched that He, may He be glorified, forgives sins for some people and some of them for others; or the address of "some" is to the people of Noah, peace be upon him, and the address of "all" is to this nation. No one has held that partition does not conflict with totality. The Sharif did not approve of his refutation of it, saying: "There is a point to examine, for al-Radi explicitly stated that there is no contradiction between them, when he said: Even if it is also an address to one nation, forgiveness of some sins does not contradict forgiveness of all of them; rather, non-forgiveness of some of them contradicts forgiveness of all of them." The saying of al-Radi is not acceptable, for what you have come to know is that the meaning of the partitive is mere partiality. [End of quotation]

The grammarians' statement, "or the address of some to the people of Noah, peace be upon him, and the address of all to this nation," was objected to on the grounds that the report of forgiveness of some occurs in several places, among them His saying in surah Ibrahim: 10, ﴿He calls you that He may forgive you of your sins﴾; among them in surah al-Ahqaf: 31, ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in Him; He will forgive you of your sins﴾; and among them what is here, which was said regarding the people of Noah, peace be upon him. As for what is mentioned in al-Ahqaf, it was said regarding the jinn; and what occurs in Ibrahim was said regarding the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, as the context makes clear. So how can what they said be valid? It was said that "min" was used in address to disbelievers rather than believers throughout the Qur'an, to distinguish between the two addresses.

It was explained that where forgiveness occurs in address to disbelievers, it is conditioned upon faith, and where it occurs in address to believers, it is accompanied by obedience, avoidance of disobedience and the like; so it encompasses the leaving of wrongs. It was objected that this distinction is complete only if the address to disbelievers did not come in general terms, and it has come in that way, as in surah al-Anfal: 38, ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven for them﴾. We have already outlined what relates to this matter, so take heed and reflect.

﴿And He will defer you to a specified term﴾ is the furthest limit that God, may He be exalted, has decreed on condition of faith and obedience, beyond what He, mighty and majestic, has decreed for them should they remain in disbelief and disobedience. For the description of the term as "specified" and the making of their deferment dependent upon faith and obedience is explicit that they have another term which they will not exceed if they do not believe; and this is what is meant by His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed the term of God﴾, that is, what He, mighty and majestic, has decreed for you on the assumption that you remain as you are, ﴿when it comes﴾ while you are as you are, ﴿is not deferred﴾. So hasten to faith and obedience before it comes, so that its condition, which is your remaining in disbelief and disobedience, is not fulfilled; then it will not come, and the condition of deferment to the specified term is fulfilled, and you will be deferred until then.

It is also permitted that by it is meant the time of the coming of the punishment mentioned in His saying, may He be glorified, ﴿before a painful punishment comes upon them﴾, for it is a term definitely fixed for it. In any case, there is no contradiction between "He will defer you" and "the term of God, when it comes, is not deferred," as is imagined. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding this, in substance, that the term is of two kinds: the term of God, whose ruling is the ruling of what is known, and what is meant by it is the specified term which is the last of the terms; and the sentence, according to him, is a justification for what is understood from His, may He be glorified, making deferment dependent upon the specified term, namely that deferment does not go beyond it. But the first is what is relied upon, for the apparent meaning is that the sentence is a justification for the command to worship, which entails forgiveness and deferment until the specified term; so the negated thing at the coming of the term must be the promised deferment. How then can it be conceived that what is supposed to come is the specified term, which is the last of the terms?

﴿If you only knew﴾, that is: if you were of the people of knowledge, you would hasten to what I command you, but you are not of its people in any way, and therefore you do not hasten. So the answer to "law" (if) relates to the beginning of the statement, and it is permitted that it relates to its end, that is: if you were of the people of knowledge, you would know that, namely that the term is not deferred when its appointed time comes. The verb in both cases is treated as intransitive. It is also permitted that it is omitted for the sake of generality, that is: if you knew anything. The first was preferred, since it does not need an estimated element. Combining the past and present forms is to indicate the continuation of the negation understood from "law." And taking the negated knowledge to be theoretical knowledge, not necessary knowledge, nor what encompasses it, for that is not negated except by way of exaggeration, God forbid.

ۘ﴿He said﴾: that is, Noah, peace be upon him, conversing with his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and recounting to Him, glorified is He, with the intent of complaint. He, glorified is He, knows best his condition: what passed between him and his people of speech and counter-speech over those long periods, after he had expended the utmost effort in the call and had gone to every known limit in warning, and his means were exhausted and his excuses failed him. ﴿My Lord, I have called my people﴾ to faith and obedience ﴿night and day﴾: that is, constantly, without slackening or lethargy.

﴿But my call has only increased them in flight﴾ — that is, away from what I called them to. Attributing the increase to the call is an attribution to the cause, in the manner of the attribution in "your seeing has gladdened me" (sarratni ru'yatuka).

(wa-firaran) — it is said to be a tamyiz (specification), and it is said to be a second object (maf'ul thani), based on the view that the verbs of increase and decrease take two objects. It has been said that this is not established, although some have mentioned it. The verse contains eloquent intensifications. The original wording would have been "they did not answer me" or the like, but this was expressed instead by the increase of flight, attributed to the call, and it was made to fall upon them, together with the use of both negation and affirmation.

**Al-Alusi's Commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 71, Verse 7**

﴿And indeed, whenever I call them﴾, meaning: to faith. The object of the verb is omitted. It is also permissible to treat the verb as intransitive, placing it in the position of the intransitive (lazim). The clause is coordinated (ʿatf) with what precedes it. This is not a case of coordinating the detailed (mufassal) with the summary (mujmal), as some have supposed, such that one would say the waw belongs to the reported speech and not to what is reported. ﴿That You may forgive them﴾, meaning: on account of faith. ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾

[p. 72]

That is, they stopped up their hearing so as not to listen to the call. This is a kinaya (metonymy) for what has been mentioned, and there is nothing preventing it from being taken literally. Attributing the act of putting to the fingers, when it is actually done by some of them, and choosing the word "putting" (ja'l) over "inserting" (idkhal), is of obvious significance. ﴿And they covered themselves with their garments﴾, meaning: they went to great lengths to wrap themselves in them, as if they asked their garments to cover them so that they would not see him, out of their extreme aversion to looking at him because of their intense dislike of the call. The expression in the form of istif'al carries an evident emphasis, and likewise the generalization of the instrument of sight and the rest of the body to being covered is an emphasis in displaying aversion. Thus the verse contains emphasis both in manner and in extent.

It has been said: they went to these lengths so that he, peace be upon him, would not recognize them and call them. But this is weak, for it has been objected that this is contradicted by its being consequent upon his words ﴿whenever I call them﴾. Except that it may be taken as a majaz (figurative use) for the intention of calling, but this is a reversal of the matter and a disruption of the composition. ﴿And they persisted﴾, meaning: they devoted themselves to disbelief and sins, were immersed in them, and strove in them. It is a isti'ara (metaphor) taken from the phrase "the donkey persisted over the herd of wild asses" (asarra al-himar ʿala al-ʿana), when he raises and stretches out his ears straight, and turns toward them, biting and driving them away. In this there is the utmost censure of them.

It is related from Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari): if there were nothing in the commission of sins except the comparison to a donkey, that alone would be sufficient as a disgrace; how much more so when the comparison is at its worst state, which is the state of biting and mounting. As for the metaphor mentioned, it has been said that this is in the original linguistic sense, while "persistence" has become a conventional literal meaning for insistence in a sin and immersion in a matter. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: iṣrar (persistence) is the entanglement in a sin, its intensification, and refusal to desist from it; its root is from ṣarr, meaning binding tightly. Perhaps this does not contradict what preceded, based on the view that the first root is binding and the second root is what you heard first. ﴿And they were arrogant﴾, meaning: against following me and obeying me, ﴿with great arrogance﴾. **Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verses 8–9:**

﴿Then indeed I called to them openly.﴾ ﴿Then indeed I declared to them, and I confided to them in secret confiding.﴾ That is: I called them time after time and repeatedly, in various manners and with differing methods. This is a generalization of the modes of the call after the generalization of the times. His saying ﴿Then indeed I called to them openly﴾ implies that openness (*jahr*) was preceded by secrecy (*sirr*). This is the most fitting reading for one whose concern is that they respond, because it is closer to achieving that, given the gentleness it contains toward the one being called. Thus *thumma* (then) serves to mark the difference between the modes. Openness is more intense than secrecy, and combining the two is more severe than using only one.

Some eminent scholars said: There is nothing in the noble text that requires that the first call was secret only. It seems he derived this from the contrast, from the placing forward of his saying (*laylan*, "by night"), from his addressing them by the title of "his people," and from his saying (*firaran*, "in flight"), since nearness is suitable to that.

He also permitted that *thumma* be understood in its literal meaning, which is temporal sequence (*al-tarakhi al-zamani*), but with reference to the beginning and end of each of secrecy and openness, and with reference to the end of combining them together, so that it does not contradict the earlier generality of times. This consideration is good, even if one takes their generality as customary, as in the saying "he does not put the staff down from his shoulder."

(*Jihaaran*) is in the accusative governed by *da'awtuhum*, functioning as a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), because it is one of the two types of calling, just as *al-qurfusa'* is put in the accusative in the saying *qa'adtu al-qurfusa'a 'alayha* ("I sat in the qurfusa' position"), because it is one of the kinds of sitting. Alternatively, *da'awtuhum* may be taken to mean *jahartu-hum* ("I called them openly"). Or it may be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a calling, open," i.e., *mujaahaaran* (openly, with the *ha'* vowelled with a fatha). Or it may be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning *mujaahiran* ("openly"), in the pattern of the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 10–11:

﴿So I said: Seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ by repentance from disbelief and sins, for He, glory be to Him, does not ( forgive that He be associated with ) [al-Nisa' 48, 116]. And your Lord said, as a means of stirring the motive for seeking forgiveness: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving﴾, constantly and abundantly forgiving to those who repent. As though they made excuses and said: If we are upon the truth, how should we abandon it; and if we are upon falsehood, how would He accept us and show kindness to us, may He, exalted is He, after we have devoted ourselves to it for a long time? So He commanded them with what erases what had passed of their sins and brings them benefits. For this reason He promised them, in return for seeking forgiveness, things that are dearer to them and more effective in their hearts than the otherworldly matters, I mean what is contained in ﴿He will send down the sky﴾ etc. And I answered them accordingly, because of what they were created with of love for worldly matters.

The soul is inclined to love of what is immediate. Qatadah said: "They were people of love for this world, so He summoned them to the Hereafter by the path they love." It was also said: when they denied him, upon him be blessings and peace, after repeated calling, God Most High withheld the rain from them and rendered the wombs of their women barren for forty years, and it was said seventy years. So He promised them that if they believed, God Most High would grant them abundance and remove from them what they were in.

This is His saying: ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant downpour﴾,
i.e., abundant in flowing. Ibn Abi Hatim? [note: not in source; omitted]

"Sky" (al-sama') is used for rain and for plants as well, as in the verse of poetry:

When the sky descends upon a people's land, we pasture upon it, even if they are angry.

It is also permitted that it be understood as "canopy" (al-mizalla), as you have heard more than once; it is masculine and feminine, and its feminine form does not prevent describing it with mid-rar (abundant). However, all intensive forms, as Sibawayh explicitly stated, are shared between masculine and feminine. In al-Bahr it is said that mif'al does not take the feminine ta' except rarely.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 12:

﴿And He will increase you in wealth and children, and will make for you gardens﴾ that is, orchards, ﴿and will make for you﴾ therein, or in general, ﴿rivers﴾ flowing.

He repeated the verb of making (ja'ala) rather than saying "will make for you gardens and rivers," because the two are different: the first is something in which their own action has a part, unlike the second. For this reason He said, ﴿will increase you in wealth and children﴾ and did not repeat the governing verb. This is what has been said, and it is, as you see, not convincing.

Perhaps the better view is that the repetition is for the sake of giving attention to the matter of the rivers, since they have an ordinary and largely causal role in the existence of the gardens and in their continuance, along with other evident benefits. And in consideration of their causal role in the continuance of the gardens, which is more important than their mere existence, and given the strength of this causal role, it was placed after them. As for omitting the repetition of the governing verb with the children, it is either because it is the original (principle), or because, since increase (imdad) is most often mentioned in connection with what is loved, and the lovableness of each of wealth and children is not complete without the other, it omitted repeating the governing verb between them, to indicate that the favour bestowed through each is not spoiled by the loss of the other.

As for placing the children later, it has been said that this is because the continuance of wealth is generally through them, especially among the people of the desert, together with a hint that wealth ultimately passes to them, which is something that gladdens the one who possesses wealth, as is not hidden. So reflect.

Al-Biqa'i said: What is meant by the gardens and rivers is what is in the Hereafter. However, the majority hold the first view. It is narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Subayh that a man came to al-Hasan and complained to him of drought, and he said to him: "Seek forgiveness from God, the Exalted." Another came to him and complained of poverty, and he said to him: "Seek forgiveness from God, the Exalted." Another came to him and said: "Pray to God, glorified is He, that He grant me a son," and he said to him: "Seek forgiveness from God, the Exalted." Another came to him and complained of the drying up of his orchards, and he said to him: "Seek forgiveness from God, the Exalted." It was said to him: "Men came to you complaining of various things and asking for various kinds, and you commanded them all to seek forgiveness!" He said: "I did not say anything from myself; I only took as evidence the word of God, the Mighty and Majestic, related concerning His Prophet Noah, peace be upon him, that he said to his people: ﴿Seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ ... the verse."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 13:

﴿What is the matter with you, that you do not hope for dignity from Allah?﴾ This is a rebuke against there being any cause for them, in their not hoping in Allah, the Exalted. (Waqaran) — here the hope (raja') is taken in the sense of fear (khawf), as al-Tasturi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who answered with it the question of Nafi' ibn al-Azraq, reciting the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"When the bees sting him, he does not hope for their sting, and he has sworn to them, in a house of wool, [that he will not harm] the honey-bees."

Or (waqaran is understood) in the sense of belief (i'tiqad), as Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and a group transmitted from him. He expressed it by "hope," which follows the lowest degree of assumption, as an intensification. "La tarjuna" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the addressees, and its governing element is the sense of settledness in (lakum). The rebuke is directed at the cause alone, while the content of the circumstantial clause is established, not at both together. "Lillah" is connected to an implied element that functions as a circumstantial clause from (waqaran). Had it been placed later, it would have been a qualifier of it. Waqar, as a group transmitted from the Habr (Ibn 'Abbas) reported, means greatness ('azamah), because, as al-Khafaji related from al-Intisaf, it occurs in the description of Allah, the Exalted, with this meaning, either directly, or because it means deliberateness (ta'ada), but that is not fitting for Him, glory be to Him, so it is applied with regard to its ultimate purpose and what results from it of greatness, either in reality or in the hearts of people. That is: what cause has come about for you while you are not fearing Allah, the Exalted, nor believing in Him as possessing a greatness that necessitates glorifying Him, glory be to Him, by faith in Him, exalted is His majesty, and obedience to Him, the Exalted.

﴿And He has created you in stages.﴾ That is, while you are in a state wholly contrary to the one you are in, namely that you know He, Mighty and Majestic, created you, bringing you through the stages of the elements, then nutrients, then humors, then drops of semen, then clots, then lumps of flesh, then bones and flesh, and then another creation. Failing to revere One whose matter is this, in His overpowering power and complete beneficence, while knowing this, is hardly something a rational person would do. Thus the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿you do not hope﴾, confirming the denunciation. The word *aṭwār* means the differing states.

They cited the poet's words:

*"If he has recovered, his blindness has flown away, and a man is created in stage after stage."*

Interpreting it as the states you have heard about, which a group of scholars has adopted, and which Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid's reports imply, although they mention only the drop, the clot, and the lump. It has also been said that the meaning is the varying states from birth to death: childhood, youth, middle age, old age, strength, and weakness. It has been said that they include variations in colors, forms, characters, and the differing religious communities.

It has also been said that they include health and sickness, the completeness and deficiency of limbs, wealth and poverty, and the like. Furthermore, it has been said that *al-rajāʾ* here means hope (*amal*), as is its well-known basic sense, and *al-waqār* means veneration (*tawqīr*), as *al-salām* means *al-taslīm* (greeting). By it is meant glorification (*taʿẓīm*). The phrase *lillāh* then serves as an explanation (*bayān*) of the one who is venerated and glorified. It is thus the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtadaʾ*), meaning "my intention is for God," or it is related to an omitted element that the mentioned word explains, meaning "veneration for God." It is not connected to the mentioned word, based on what some have upheld, that the complement of a verbal noun (*maʿmūl al-maṣdar*) may not precede it in any case, and that if it were placed after it, it would be a complement (*ṣila*) of it, as in the *Kashshāf*.

In it there is also the meaning: "Why do you not stand in a state in which you hope that God, Mighty and Majestic, will honor you in the abode of reward?" The sum of this is: "Why do you not hope to be venerated and glorified?" with the verb in the passive, so that it is as though it were said: "By whom is veneration [given]?", i.e., "Who is it that glorifies us, and whose glorification of us is specific to Him?" So it is said: "God." He explained it by saying "in a state," etc., as an indication that they should be deluded by their own condition, as though it were said: "Why are you deluded, not hoping?"

He made the urging to hope a metonymy (*kināyah*) for urging faith and righteous deeds, because hope requires the establishment of the causes, unlike delusion (*ghurūr*). It is an allusive metonymy (*kināyah īmāʾiyyah*), since there is no intermediary. Had it been made a symbolic metonymy (*kināyah ramziyyah*), owing to the obscurity of the distinction between hope and delusion for most people, it would have been a valid view, as stated in *al-Kashf*. The Mufti of the Ottoman lands, may God have mercy on him, objected to this, saying that the non-hope of disbelievers in God's glorifying them in the abode of reward is not in the category of being unlikely or denied. Moreover, reading *al-waqār* as *al-tawqīr* is far-fetched, and reading *lillāh* as an explanation of the one venerated, and the claim that if it were placed after it, it would be a complement of *al-waqār*, is contradictory, as is clear. For its being an explanation of the one venerated requires that the veneration proceed from God, and the *waqār* be an attribute of those addressed; and its being a complement of *al-waqār* requires that the veneration proceed from them, and the *waqār* be an attribute of Him, Mighty and Majestic. End of quotation.

It may be answered regarding the matter of contradiction that when you say *ḍarb li-Zaydin* (a striking for Zayd), it is possible that Zayd is the agent or that he is the object, and the validity of both annexations suffices as proof. So when it is placed after, it is possible that *al-waqār*, in the sense of *al-tawqīr*, proceeds from Him, Exalted, so that *al-waqār* is an attribute of those addressed; and it is possible that it is related to Him, so that the veneration proceeds from them and the *waqār* is an attribute of Him, Exalted. The utmost in this matter is that, since *lillāh* was placed first and its relation to the later verbal noun was prevented, it became an explanation, and the context indicated the intention that the veneration proceed from Him, Mighty and Majestic. How is this contradiction? Yes, the discussion remains about the indicator, and perhaps it is the context, based on the notion that the people found it unlikely that they would be accepted and that God would show them kindness if they abandoned their falsehood. This would be part of completing the removal of the doubt in what you have heard of their saying: "How would He accept us and show kindness to us?" etc. From this answer it is known that the claim that the non-hope of disbelievers in God's glorifying them is not in the category of unlikelihood is as is not hidden. Some have said that God's words ﴿And He has created you﴾ up to His words, glorified is He, ﴿wide roads﴾ serve to show that He, may His majesty be exalted, never ceases to bestow favors upon you despite your disbelief, so how would He not show kindness to you and venerate you if you believe?

The *aṭwār* are explained as the various matters that befall a person in the course of his ages, such as childhood, youth, middle age, and others, some of which occur while in disbelief and are suitable to be cited as a favor. It is also required that the return to the earth be one of their blessings, based on the idea that it conceals the hideousness of bodies in the easiest manner after the inevitable arrival of death in this life. Fairness, after all this, requires that one admit, whether it is accepted or not, that the aforementioned interpretation is forced and far, by great distances, from the apparent sense.

It has been said: the meaning is "Why do you not fear God, Exalted, in forbearance and in holding back from hastening punishment, so that you believe?" So *al-rajāʾ* means fear (*khawf*) and *al-waqār* means forbearance (*ḥilm*) literally, as is the apparent sense of al-Rāghib's words, or metaphorically (*isti ʿārah*) for it, because both share the second meaning, or figuratively (*majāz*), since forbearance does not normally separate from *waqār*. In a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, it is explained as consequence (*ʿāqibah*), where he said: "that is, you do not fear for God any consequence," and this is then a metonymy, taking *al-waqār* in the sense of steadfastness (*thabāt*). From Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk it is reported that the meaning is "Why do you not care about God's greatness?" Qutrub said:

*"This is the dialect of the people of Ḥijāz, Hudhayl, Khuzāʿah, and Muḍar; they say lam arjū, meaning lam ubāli (I did not care)."*

The most apparent of the meanings is the one we mentioned first.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verses 15–16:

When he had mentioned some of the signs within the souls, he followed them with some of the signs of the horizons. Because one of the two matters is far removed from the other in rank, he did not join them with a conjunction but broke off and said: ﴿Do you not see how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ That is, placed one above another in conformity. The meaning of conformity (tatabuq) is agreement in beauty, in containing wisdom, and in excellence of making. ﴿You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾ (Al-Mulk: 3) is a departure from the apparent sense, on which the reports agree, without any reason requiring it. ﴿And made the moon a light within them﴾, illuminating the face of the earth in the darkness of the night. He made it "within them" even though it is in one of them, the lowest heaven, as one says, "Zayd is in Baghdad" while he is in a district of it. What favours this is brevity, the relation of the whole and the part, and the fact that the heavens are in layers and transparent.

﴿And made the sun a lamp﴾, which removes the darkness of the night, and by its light the people of the world see the face of the earth and observe the horizons, just as the people of a house see by the light of a lamp what they need to see. Its tanwin (the indefinite ending "-an") is for glorification.

In the passage there is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh). Because the lamp is better known and closer, it was made the likened-to (al-mushabbah bihi). Because the notion of extending to others is included in its meaning, unlike the light (nur), it was more eloquent than it. Perhaps in likening the sun to a standing lamp whose light is its own, not by way of reflection, there is a symbol that its light is not reflected to it from another star, just as the light of the moon is reflected onto it from the sun, owing to the variation of its phases by nearness and distance from it, along with its eclipse when the earth comes between them. The astronomers of the old cosmology (ahl al-hay'a al-qadimah) affirmed this. In a report which I think is sound, the light of the sun is poured upon it from the Throne. I think that whoever says it revolves around another star among the astronomers of the new cosmology also holds that it derives its light from something else.

Then, the apparent meaning is that the intended sense is "and made the sun within them." It is said that it is in the lowest heaven, in an orbit within its thickness. It is also said that it is in the fourth heaven, which is the view best known among the earlier astronomers, and they supported it with what is recorded in their books. In al-Bahr (the tafsir of Abu Hayyan) there is a report of a view that it is in the fifth, but this hardly holds. Among the things that make children laugh, let alone the mature scholars of gnosis, is what is also reported there: that it is in the fourth in winter and in the seventh in summer. The later astronomers held that it is the centre of the planets, and they counted the earth among them but did not count the moon, because it revolves around the earth, and it is, in their view, between the earth and the sun. God willing, we shall compose a treatise on verifying the truth, and the truth is clearer than the sun to those who possess it.

﴿And Allah caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾, meaning He brought you into being from it. The verb "to cause to grow" (*anbata*) is used metaphorically (*istiʿārah*) for "to bring into being" (*ins̱āʾ*), because growth is more indicative of coming-into-existence and formation from the earth, since it is something perceived by the senses and its occurrence has been repeated. Although they did not deny origination, by denying the resurrection they were treated as though they denied it. So in the speech there is an explicit metaphor (*istiʿārah taṣrīḥiyyah*) of the following type (*tabaʿiyyah*). The particle *min* ("from") is an initial particle (*ibtidāʾiyyah*, indicating the starting point), governing the remote origin. As for *nabātan* ("as a growth"), Abu Ḥayyān and a group said it is an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar muʾakkid*) for *anbatakum*, with the augmentations dropped, and the original form is *inbātan*. Or it is in the accusative by supposing a verb: "so you grew, a growth" (*fa-nabattum nabātan*). In *al-Kashshāf* it is stated that *inbāt* and *nabāt* are of the active and passive type (*fiʿl* and *infiʿāl*), and they are one in reality; the difference is relative to what subsists in the agent and what subsists in the recipient. Therefore there is no need to include (*taḍmīn*) another verb or to supply one.

Then, if *inbāt* is taken in its lexical meaning, there is no need for supplying anything, since it itself already implies *nabāt* (growth), as we have indicated. Thus *nabātan* is in the accusative by virtue of this implicit inclusion. But if it is taken in its customary usage, applying it to the preliminary stage of growth, such as the burying of seed in the earth for example, then the proper course is to understand the meaning as: "He caused you to grow, so you grew a growth," so that there is in it an indication of a point similar to the nuance found in the Exalted saying ﴿so it gushed forth﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 160] (*fa-nbajasat*), namely indicating power and the swiftness with which His command takes effect.

It is also permitted that the original be: "He caused you to grow from the earth a growth (*inbātan*), so you grew a growth (*nabātan*)." Then the verbal noun was omitted from the first clause and the verb from the second, relying on what was mentioned in the other. This is on the basis of the device of *iḥtibāk* (balanced omission). Al-Qāḍī said: "He abbreviated, relying on the implicative indication (*al-dalālah al-iltizāmiyyah*)." Al-Khafājī said that this contains, as he stated, the poetry mentioned, so reflect upon it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 18:

﴿Then He will return you into it﴾, i.e., into the earth, by burial at the time of your death,
Page 76
﴿and bring you out﴾ from it at the Resurrection and the Gathering, ﴿a [sure] bringing out﴾, certain, with no doubt about it. He joined ﴿yuʿiduku﴾ (He returns you) with ﴿thumma﴾ (then), because of the lengthy interval of time between the creation and the returning, in which the obligation occurs, by which they deserve the recompense after the return. He joined ﴿yukhrijukum﴾ (He brings you out) with the conjunction ﴿wa﴾ (and), not ﴿thumma﴾, even though the bringing out is likewise, because the states of the barzakh (intermediate state) and the Hereafter are regarded as one thing, so it is as if it were a single matter. It is not permissible that some of it be certain to occur and some not; rather, the whole matter must inevitably take place, even if it is delayed beyond the initial production.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verses 19–20:

﴿And Allah has made for you the earth a spread-out carpet﴾ [you] move about upon it as one moves upon a carpet. There is no indication in this that the earth is flat and not spherical, as is the case with the sea and other things, because a great sphere is such that everyone upon it sees what is near him as flat. Moreover, belief in the sphericity of the earth or its opposite is not a matter that is obligatory in the Sharia. Yet its sphericity is like a certainty, even if it is not in reality. As for the placement of ﴿lakum﴾ (for you) between the verb "made" (ja'ala) and its explicit object, the reason for it is known from what has passed more than once. ﴿That you may traverse therefrom roads﴾ (subul), ﴿broad highways﴾ (fijaj), wide ones. It is the plural of fajj, so it is an adjectival form (sifah mushabbahah) functioning as an epithet (na't) for subul.

Others have said: it is a noun for the wide road. It has also been said: it is a noun for a passage between two mountains, in which case it is a substitute (badal) or an explicative appositive (ʿatf bayan). The word "min" (from) is connected to what precedes it, because the verb includes the meaning of "taking" (ittikhadh); otherwise it would be followed by "fi" or by an implied particle. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿subulan﴾, meaning: roads existing from the earth. Had it been placed later, it would have been an epithet for them.
