**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 21:**

﴿Nuh said﴾: The narrative formula was repeated because of the long time since the account of his private supplication to his Lord, Exalted and Majestic. That is, he (peace be upon him) said while whispering to Him, Exalted is He, complaining to Him, Exalted and Majestic: ﴿My Lord, they have disobeyed me﴾, that is, they persisted in disobeying me in what I commanded them, even though I exerted myself in guiding them with admonition and reminder. ﴿And they followed one whose wealth and children increased him in nothing but loss﴾, that is, they continued to follow their leaders, whom their wealth had made arrogant and whom their children had deceived, and this became a cause of increased loss for them in the Hereafter, so they became a model for them in loss. The apparent meaning is that the following of their common folk and lowly ones of these leaders, and the description of them by this, indicates that they followed them because of the standing (wajahah) they gained through wealth and children, not because of any doubt they saw in them that would justify following them in general.

And Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-A'raj, Mujahid, al-Akhawan (the two brothers), Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Nafi' in the transmission of Kharijah from him read ﴿wulduhu﴾ (with a ḍamma on the wāw and a sukūn on the lām). It is said that it is a singular, a dialectal form of *walad* with both letters vocalized with a fatḥa, like *al-ḥuzn* and *al-ḥazan*. It is also said that it is a plural of it, like *al-asad* and *al-usd*. In the Qamus (the dictionary of al-Fayruzabadi): "*al-walad* with a fatḥa on the wāw and lām, and with a ḍamma or kasra, is singular and plural, and it may be pluralized as *awlad* and *wilda*, and *walida* with a kasra, and *wuld* with a ḍamma." End of quotation.

And al-Hasan also read it with a kasra and a sukūn, as did al-Jahdari, Qatadah, Dharr, Talhah, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu 'Amr in one transmission.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 22:

﴿And they schemed﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with the relative clause (ṣilah) of "man" (those who). The plural is used in view of its meaning, just as the singular in the earlier pronouns is used in view of its wording. In this there is an indication of their gathering together in scheming, so that it would be more intense and greater. It has also been said that it is coordinated with ﴿they disobeyed me﴾, but the first is more suitable, because it indicates that the leaders added misguidance to error, and this fits the context better, for what immediately appears is that what follows is also a description of the chiefs. Taking that coordination to mean that "some of them schemed against others and some of them said to others" is contrary to what immediately appears.

﴿a tremendous scheme﴾, that is, great to the utmost extent, so it is of the forms of intensification (ṣiyagh al-mubalaghah). ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar said: it is a Yemeni dialect, and upon it is the saying of the poet:

A fair one who hunts hearts and captivates with her beauty the heart of the Muslim reciter,

and his saying:

A man is joined to the youths of generosity by the character of the noble, not by ablution (wiḍaʾ).

Some of the rude Bedouins heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting this verse and said: "How eloquent your Lord is, O Muhammad!" And if the tanwin in "makran" is taken as for emphasis (tafkhim), the matter of intensification in their scheming increases, that is, great to the utmost extent. This is their deceit in religion, their turning people away from it, and their enticing and inciting them to harm Noah, peace be upon him.

ʿIsa, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu al-Simal read "kubaran" with the bāʾ lightened, and this is also a form of intensification, but it is less than the intensified form. Similar to kubar in this are ḥisan, ṭiwal, ʿujab and jumal, and many other words. Zayd ibn ʿAli and Ibn Muhaysin, as transmitted from him by Wahb ibn Waḍiḥ, read "kibaran" with the kasra on the kāf and the fatḥa on the bāʾ. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a plural of kabir, as if he made "makran" stand in place of "dhunub" (sins) or "af'al" (deeds), and for this reason it was described with the plural.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 23:

﴿And they said: Do not abandon your gods﴾ meaning: do not leave off their worship at all in favor of the worship of the Lord of Nuh, peace be upon him. ﴿Nor abandon Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, Ya'uq, and Nasr﴾ meaning: do not leave off the worship of these. He singled them out for mention although they are included in what preceded because they were the greatest of their idols and false objects of worship, and the most important of them in their eyes, even though they varied in greatness among themselves in their claim, as indicated by the repetition of "nor" with some and its omission with another. It has been said that he made Yaghuth and Ya'uq and Nasr separate from the negation because of the frequent repetition of "lā" and to avoid confusion. These idols later passed on to the Arabs.

Al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The idols that were among the people of Nuh, peace be upon him, came to the Arabs afterward. As for Wadd, it belonged to the tribe of Kalb at Dawmat al-Jandal. As for Suwa', it belonged to Hudhayl. As for Yaghuth, it belonged to Murad, then to the Banu Ghutayf near Saba'. As for Ya'uq, it belonged to Hamdan. As for Nasr, it belonged to Himyar, to the family of Dhu al-Kala'. These names were the names of righteous men from the people of Nuh. When they perished, Satan inspired their people: "Set up in their assemblies where they used to sit idols, and name them after their names." They did so, and they were not worshipped until those people died and knowledge was forgotten, and then they were worshipped.

Abu al-Shaykh, in al-'Azamah, narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: Adam, peace be upon him, had five sons: Wadd, Suwa', etc. They were worshipers, and a man among them died, and they grieved over him greatly. Satan came to them and said: "Do you grieve for this companion of yours?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Would you like me to make an image of him in your qiblah, so that when you look at it you remember him?" They said: "We dislike that you place in our qiblah something we would pray toward." He said: "Then I will place it at the back of the mosque." They said: "Yes." So he made an image of him for them until all five died, and he made their images at the back of the mosque. Then the things diminished, until they abandoned the worship of God, the Exalted, and worshipped these. So God, the Exalted, sent Nuh, peace be upon him, who called them to worship God alone and to abandon the worship of these. They said what they said.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that Wadd was the eldest and the most righteous of them, and that they were all sons of Adam, peace be upon him.

It is also reported that Wadd was the first object of worship besides God, the Exalted. 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Mutahhir, who said: They mentioned in the presence of Abu Ja'far, may God be pleased with him, Yazid ibn al-Muhallab. He said: "Indeed, he was killed in the first land in which something other than God, the Exalted, was worshipped." Then he mentioned Wadd and said: He was a Muslim man and was beloved among his people. When he died, they gathered around his grave in the land of Babil and grieved for him. When Iblis saw their grief, he took the form of a man and said: "I see your grief over this. Would you like me to make an image of him for you, so that it may be in your assembly and you may remember him through it?" They said: "Yes." So he made an image of him for them, and they placed it in their assembly and began to remember him through it. When he saw how much they remembered him, he said: "Would you like me to place for each of you an image of him in his house, so that he may be remembered through it?" They said: "Yes." So he did, and they began to remember him through it. Their children grew up and saw what they did with it, and they multiplied, and the purpose of remembering him was forgotten, until they took him as a god worshipped besides God, the Exalted. So Wadd was the first to be worshipped besides God in the earth.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi that he said: I saw Yaghuth, and it was of lead. It was carried on a bare-backed camel, and they traveled with it without urging it on, until it was the one that knelt down. When they dismounted, they said: "It has been pleased with you as a resting place," and they would camp around it and build a structure over it.

It has been said that the physical idols themselves are unlikely to have survived and passed to the Arabs, so apparently only the names remained, and the Arabs made idols and named them with them, and they said also "Abd Wadd" and "Abd Yaghuth," meaning their idols. What Abu 'Uthman saw of them was named after what had passed.

It is related that Wadd was in the form of a man, Suwa' was in the form of a woman, Yaghuth was in the form of a lion, Ya'uq was in the form of a horse, and Nasr was in the form of a vulture. This contradicts what was mentioned earlier, that they were in the forms of righteous men, and that is the more sound view.

Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Shaybah, with a variant from them, read «Wuddan» with a damma on the waw. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read «wa-lā Yaghūthan wa-Ya'ūqan» with tanwin on both. The author of al-Lawami' said: He made them both to be of the pattern fa'ul, and therefore he gave them tanwin. In the reading of the majority they are two adjectives derived from al-ghawth and al-'awq, following the pattern yaf'ulu from them, and they are definite, and therefore they are not given tanwin, because of the combination of the two weights: definiteness and resemblance to the imperfect verb. Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying: This is confused. Firstly, it is impossible that they be fa'ul, because the root of yaghuth is nonexistent, and likewise ya'uq. Secondly, they are not adjectives, because the pattern yaf'ulu does not occur as a noun or adjective; they were excluded from tanwin only for definiteness and the pattern of the verb, if they are Arabic, and for definiteness and foreignness, if they are foreign.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Al-A'mash read «wa-lā Yaghūthan wa-Ya'ūqan» with tanwin, and this is an error, because definiteness is obligatory, and likewise the pattern of the verb. You know that al-A'mash was not alone in this, and it is not an error. They have been explained on one of two aspects. The first is that the tanwin is for harmony, as they said in «salāsilan wa-aghlālan», and this is a kind of mushakalah counted among the embellishments. The second is that it comes in the dialect of those who give tanwin to all that is not declinable, contrary to the common Arabs, and this is a dialect related by al-Kisa'i and others. But it is objected to this that it is a non-eloquent dialect, and it is not fitting to base an explanation upon it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 24:

﴿And they have certainly led astray﴾, that is, the leaders, ﴿many﴾, a great multitude of people, that is, before these who were enjoined to cling to the worship of idols. So they are not the first whom they have led astray. The past tense and its connection with "qad" (certainly) indicate this, for it implies that their misguidance continued until the time of the report about the misguidance of the last group. It is also permitted that by "many" be meant these enjoiners, although the apparent wording would have been "and the leaders have led them astray", meaning the enjoined addressees in His saying ﴿Do not leave your gods﴾. Instead, "many" is placed in the position of that, by way of abstraction (tajrid).

Al-Hasan said: "And they have certainly led astray" means the idols, so it is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿My Lord, they have led many of the people astray﴾ (Ibrahim: 36). The pronoun used for rational beings is because the idols were given the status of rational beings in their eyes and according to their belief. Al-Bahr supports this by noting that the pronoun returns to the nearest previous mention. But it is not hidden that returning it to the leaders is more apparent, since they are the ones being spoken about, and the meaning is more applicable to them. The clause is said to be circumstantial (ḥāliyya) or conjoined to what precedes it.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers except in error﴾, it is said to be conjoined to ﴿My Lord, they have disobeyed me﴾ (Nuh: 21), as part of the reported speech of Nuh, peace be upon him, after "he said" (qāla), with the waw standing in for it. Its meaning is: he said, ﴿My Lord, they have disobeyed me﴾, and he said, ﴿and do not increase﴾, etc., that is, he said these two statements. In this view, the waw is part of the speech of Allah, exalted is He, since it falls within the reported speech, and what follows it is the reported content. Al-Zamakhshari adopted this view, and he only resorted to it to avoid conjoining a command (inshā') to a statement (khabar).

It is also said that it is conjoined to what precedes it, and the waw belongs to the reported speech, and the correspondence is between the imperative and the declarative, which is not a necessary condition for conjunction, as Abu Hayyan and others stated, though this is disputed. In al-Kashf, you may make it of the type of His saying ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾ (Maryam: 46), that is, ﴿so forsake them and do not increase them﴾. The shift to ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ indicates that they deserve the supplication against them, and it presents his excuse, peace be upon him, and serves as a warning and a kindness to others. It is also said that this is part of what results from their evils, and this is a fine meaning. According to this view, the conjunction is to an implied imperative clause. Perhaps the better view is that the conjunction is to ﴿My Lord, they have disobeyed me﴾, and the waw belongs to the reported speech, and the correspondence is present.

Al-Khafaji said: The apparent purpose of His saying ﴿My Lord, they have﴾ and so on is complaint, showing helplessness and despair regarding them. It is thus a request for victory over them, like His saying ﴿My Lord, help me, for they have denied me﴾ (al-Dukhan: 22). Even if he did not intend this, it would repeat what was mentioned before from him, peace be upon him. In that case it is a metonymy (kināya) for his saying "forsake them", or "help me", or "make your religion manifest", or the like. Thus it is the conjunction of an imperative to an imperative without any need for an implied element. What supports this is that Allah, exalted is He, called the like of this a supplication, when He said, ﴿So he called upon his Lord, saying: These are a criminal people﴾ (al-Dukhan: 22). Reflect on this. It is a fine view, free from forced interpretation and from adopting disputed matters, except that there is some unease in the testimony.

The error that is the object of the supplication for its increase is either the error in the promotion of their scheming and the interests of their worldly life, so that this is a supplication against them for the non-facilitation of their affairs, or the error in the sense of destruction, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness﴾ (al-Qamar: 47). This is taken from straying on a path, because whoever strays in it perishes. So the meaning is: destroy them.

Ibn Bahr explained it as punishment, which is close to what has been mentioned. It is also said that it is on its literal meaning, namely error in religion, and the supplication for its increase was only after it was revealed to him, peace be upon him, that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed. Its outcome is a supplication against them for an increase in their punishment. This requires evidence. By what you have heard, the objection is resolved, namely the objection that seeking error and the like is either impermissible absolutely, or, if it is sought in a manner of approval, and without that, even if permissible, it is not praiseworthy or pleasing. So how did Nuh, peace be upon him, supplicate with this against them?

[p. 79]

**﴿Because of their sins﴾**, that is, because of their sins **﴿they were drowned﴾** by the flood, and not because of some other matter. Here *min* is causal (*ta'lilliyyah*, indicating cause), and *ma* is extra (*za'idah*) between the preposition and the noun it governs, in order to magnify the sins, since they are among the major sins that are forbidden. Whoever does not regard it as extra makes *khaṭī'ātihim* indefinite (*nakirah*) and makes it a substitute (*badal*) for it. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah claimed that *min* is for the beginning of the end-point (*li-ibtidā' al-ghāyah*), and that is, as you see, untenable.

Abu Rajā' read *khaṭiyyātihim*, changing the hamza to a yā' and assimilating it into the following yā'. Al-Jaḥdarī and 'Ubayd, from Abu 'Amr, read *khaṭī'atihim* in the singular, with hamza. Al-Ḥasan, 'Īsā, al-A'raj (with variation from them), and Abu 'Amr read *khaṭāyāhum*, a broken plural (*jam' taksīr*). 'Abd Allāh read *min khaṭī'ātihim mā ughriqū*, with *mā* added between *khaṭī'ātihim* and *ughriqū*, and it is construed as verbal-nominal (*maṣdariyyah*), meaning: because of their sins, their drowning. Zayd ibn 'Alī read *ghuriqū* with a shadda in place of the hamza. Both of these are transmitted readings (*li-l-naql*).

**﴿So they were made to enter﴾** a fire, which is the fire of the intermediate state (*al-barzakh*). What is meant is the punishment of the grave. Whoever dies in water or fire, or is eaten by beasts or birds, for example, suffers what the buried suffer of punishment. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they were drowned on one side and burned with fire on another side. Ibn al-Anbārī recited:

*The creation is gathered at times and scattered at others,*
*and the two occurrences are arts with various states.*

*Do not marvel at opposites when they come together:*
*God brings together water and fire.*

It is possible that what is meant is the fire of the Hereafter. The sequence (*ta'qīb*) in the first reading is apparent, and on this reading it is because the interval between drowning and entering is not counted as significant. It is as if He likened the passing of an insignificant interval to the absence of any interval at all. It is also permitted that the *fā'* of sequence be used figuratively for causation, because the effect is like one that follows its cause even if it is delayed from it, owing to the absence of a condition or the presence of an obstacle. The indefiniteness of *nār* is either to magnify and terrify it, or because He, exalted and majestic, prepared for them, according to their sins, a particular kind of fire. The beauty in **﴿they were drowned, then entered﴾** fire is unmatched, and God Most High has the pearl (*durr*) of the Revelation.

**﴿And they found for themselves no helpers apart from God﴾**, that is, none of them found a single helper. This contains an allusion (*ta'rīḍ*) to their taking gods besides Him, and to the fact that those gods are unable to help them, and a mockery of them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 26:

﴿And Noah said: "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any dwelling-place of the disbelievers."﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with its like preceding it. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾ and so on, is an interjected parenthesis (iʿtirāḍ) placed between his prayer, upon him be peace, to indicate from the outset that what befell them of drowning and burning did not befall them except because of their sins, which Noah, upon him be peace, enumerated, and he pointed to their deserving destruction on account of them, not that it is a narration of the drowning and burning themselves in the manner of narrating what occurred between him, upon him be peace, and them of states and statements. Otherwise it would have been delayed until after the narration of this prayer. This was said by the Mufti of the Ottoman lands (Muftī al-Diyār al-Rūmiyya), may God have mercy on him.

As for what has been said, that it is a conjunction with "they did not find" (lam yajidū), or with the clause "Because of their sins" and so on, and that the intended meaning is not the literal supplication but rather gloating and displaying satisfaction with what their destruction was, this is extremely far-fetched. It is well known that this supplication was before their destruction.

Al-Dayyār (a dwelling-place) is among the nouns that are used only in general negation. It is said: "There is no dayyār in the house" or "dayyūr," like qayyām and qayyūm, meaning: there is no one in it. It is fayʿāl, from al-dār (the house) or from al-dawr (turning around), as if it were said: "Do not leave upon the earth of the disbelievers" anyone who would dwell in a house, or "do not leave upon it from among them anyone who turns around and moves." Its original form is daywār; the waw and the yāʾ came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukūn, so the waw was changed to yāʾ and the yāʾ was assimilated into the yāʾ. It is not faʿʿāl, for otherwise it would be dawwār, since there would then be no reason for the change.

(Min al-kāfirīn) is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to it; had it been placed later, it would have been a ṣifa (adjective) of it. By "the disbelievers" is meant his people, whom he invited to faith and obedience, but they did not respond. Now, if the people were spread out across the eastern and western regions of the earth, as they are spread today, and his mission was to some of them, such as the inhabitants of the Arabian Peninsula and those near them, then that is fine. And if they were not spread out in that way, but were rather in the Peninsula and near it, then if his mission was to some of them too, the same applies. But if his mission was to all of them, then an objection arises, namely that it entails the generality (ʿumūm) of the mission.

Some have said that it is specific to our Prophet ﷺ. It is answered that this generality is not like the generality of the mission of our Prophet ﷺ; rather, it is due to the confinement of the people of the earth to a portion of it, so it is a necessary confinement and not a generality in every respect. This is similar to what is said regarding the mission of Adam, upon him be peace, to his wife and children, for they were then nothing but like the people of one household. Moreover, it has been said that there is no difficulty even if we hold that people were then spread out as they are today, and that he was sent to all of them, because the generality specific to our Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, is the generality encompassing jinn and humankind until the Day of Resurrection, and even the angels, peace be upon them, and more. The well-known view is that he, upon him be peace, was sent to all the inhabitants of the earth, and that none of them believed except a few. He used this supplication and the generality of the Flood as evidence for this. It has been objected that the "earth" is often used to refer to a portion of it, so it is possible that it is so here. Even if we accept that the whole is intended, the supplication is against the disbelievers, and they are those to whom he was sent; he invited them and they did not respond. As for the claim that they are all others than the people of the Ark, that is the subject of the question. As for the Flood, we do not accept its generality; and even if it is accepted, it does not entail that everyone drowned in it was obligated to believe in it, upon him be peace, and sinful for abandoning it. Affliction may encompass the righteous and the wicked, but they will be returned to different destinations, as occurs in the narration of the sinking of al-Bayda. What points to this is that their children were drowned with them, as has been said.

Al-Ḥasan was asked about this, and he said: "God, exalted is He, knew their innocence, yet He destroyed them without punishment." Yes, the wisdom in the destruction of these children is an increase in punishment for their fathers and mothers, when they see their children drowning. Some have claimed that God, exalted is He, rendered the wombs of their women barren and dried up the loins of their men forty or seventy years before the Flood, so that no child was with them when they were drowned. This needs a sound transmission. The wisdoms of God, mighty and majestic, cannot be counted, so understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 71, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, if You leave them﴾, that is, on the earth, all of them or some of them, ﴿they will mislead Your servants﴾ away from the path of truth. It is likely that the intended "servants" are those who believed in him, peace be upon him, and that misleading them means turning them back to disbelief through some kind of deception. Or the intended ones are those born among them who did not reach the age of *taklif* (legal accountability) or those who will be born among those believers and called to faith, and misleading them means preventing them from faith. In some reports, a man among them would bring his son to him, peace be upon him, and say: "Beware of this one, for he is a liar, and my father enjoined on me the same advice," so the elder would die and the younger would grow up upon that. It is said that from here he, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And they will beget none but wicked, ungrateful disbelievers﴾, that is, of those who will become immoral and disbelieving. He described them by what they would become, because of his firm knowledge of this from the experience he had gained over a thousand years less fifty years. A similar statement is his saying, peace be upon him: ﴿If You leave them, they will mislead Your servants﴾. It is also said that he meant those who would be born from them and who would be wicked and disbelieving, and he knew all of this through revelation (*wahy*), as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿None of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36]. It is reported from Qatadah, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd that he, peace be upon him, did not invoke against them until Allah the Exalted had brought forth every believer from their loins and rendered the wombs of their women barren. In any case, his saying ﴿Indeed, You﴾ and so on is an apology for what might be said: that supplicating for their annihilation, while it is possible that some of their descendants would believe, is not befitting the station of the prophets, peace be upon them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 71, verse 28:**

﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾. He meant his father, Lamk ibn Matushalakh (Lamech), whose vocalization has already been given, and his mother, Shamkha, with the *shin* and *kha* marked, on the pattern of *sakra*, daughter of Unush, with the *alif* marked, on the pattern of *usul*. They were both believers, for otherwise it would not be permissible to pray for their forgiveness. It is also said that by "my parents" he meant Adam and Eve. Ibn Jubayr and al-Jahdari read «and for my father» with a *kasra* on the *dal* and a silent *ya*. In that case, either he specified his nearest father, or he meant all of his ancestors back to Adam, peace be upon him, and they did not disbelieve, as Ibn 'Abbas said: "Between Nuh and Adam, peace be upon him, there was no father who was a disbeliever." Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may Allah honour his face and be pleased with him, and Zayd ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur, al-Nakha'i and al-Zuhri read «(and for my two sons)», the dual of *walad*, meaning Sam and Ham, according to what has been said. In one report, Sam was a prophet.

﴿and for whoever enters my house﴾. It is said he meant his dwelling. It is also said he meant his ship. Al-Jumhur and Ibn 'Abbas said he meant his mosque. In a report from the scholar (al-Habr), he meant his religious law (*shari'a*), and he borrowed for it the name of "house", as they say "the dome of Islam" and "the tent-pole of religion". The most immediate meaning is the dwelling. His wife and his son Kan'an went out, and this is shown by his words ﴿believing﴾. It is also possible, as has been said, that he did not affirm the departure of Kan'an until after he had been told that "he is not of your family".

﴿and for the believing men and the believing women﴾, that is, from every nation until the Day of Resurrection. This is a generalization after a specification. He asked forgiveness of his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, to show his great need of Him, glorified is He, and out of love for those for whom he sought forgiveness, from among his parents and the believers. It is also said that he asked forgiveness when he had prayed against the disbelievers, because that is a form of vengeance against them. But it is not hidden that the context rejects this, and likewise His words ﴿and do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction﴾, that is, ruin. Mujahid said: "loss". The first meaning is more apparent.

He, peace be upon him, made two supplications: one against the disbelievers and one for the believers. Since the first was answered for him, it is not remote that the second should also be answered for him. Allah the Exalted is the most generous of the generous.

Most of the verses of this noble surah and others state clearly that those people were disbelievers who would be destroyed on the Day of Resurrection. Therefore the judgment that they were saved, as the words of the Greatest Shaykh (Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, in his *Fusus* imply, is something from which one disowns oneself before Allah the Exalted. Such is the claim that Nuh, peace be upon him, did not call them in a manner that would require their faith, along with His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. The most I say is: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents, and whoever enters my house believing, and the believing men and the believing women﴾.
